newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil on safer path than Mexico - Dornbusch.
newsitem.headline: Brazil on safer path than Mexico - Dornbusch.

text.p: Brazil may be burdened by 'mediocre' leadership, but it is on a safer path toward economic stability than Mexico, U.S.-based economist Rudiger Dornbusch said in an interview published on Friday.

"In both countries nobody knows what the government is going to do with monetary, fiscal and exchange rate policy... But I don't think the two countries are going in the same direction," Dornbusch told Brazil's Carta Capital, a financial magazine published twice a month.
"Brazil is not heading towards a crash. But Mexico can go back to having big problems," Dornbusch said.

The Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor, who has often criticized government policies in Latin America, made a market impact last year when at an international currency seminar he hinted Brazil was facing a crisis similar to Mexico's December 1994 peso crash.
Dornbusch, who correctly predicted the 1994 peso crash, was careful during the Carta Capital interview to distinguish between Latin America's two biggest important economies.
He said Mexico had more to watch out for in the short to medium term than Brazil.
Among Mexico's chief worries are politics, competitiveness and exchange rate policy, Dornbusch said.
"Day after day, Mexico is losing its competitiveness just like on the eve of both the 1982 and 1994 crises," he said, referring to the onslaught of the 1980s debt crisis and the Mexican peso crisis.
Dornbusch said Mexican officials too often adopt new rules that change the game plan for foreign and local companies, making long-term planning difficult.
He added that the Mexican government has failed to both fight inflation and maintain a competitive exchange rate. Dornbusch's answer: "They should totally abandon the peso and dollarize the economy."
Politically, Mexico is vulnerable to growing support for the leftist Democratic Revolutionary Party (PRD), whose victory in 2000 would create an "extraordinarily conflicting" situation.
While Brazil remains one of Latin America's slowest-moving reformers, it faces no serious crisis on the horizon, Dornbusch said.
"Brazil could do better, but the government and Congress have opted for mediocre performance. It is precisely because the country faces no crisis that everyone accepts mediocrity," Dornbusch said.

When asked if he thought Brazil should move more radically, like neighboring Argentina, to reform the economy and privatize state-owned companies, Dornbusch replied: "I don't think Brazil will have radical change... My worry is the opposite, that Brazil will miss out by avoiding big changes."

He referred to this week's privatization of mining giant CVRD, which will be Latin America's largest state selloff to date, as "show business." President Fernando Henrique Cardoso needed to do something highly visible to maintain his government's image as a reformer and the CVRD sale fit the bill, Dornbusch said.
While no serious crisis looms in Brazil, much remains to be done, including progress on the fiscal and reform front.
The MIT economist also criticized Brazilian exchange rate policy, which he said was subject to the whims of Central Bank International Affairs Director Gustavo Franco.

"Pay attention to what Gustavo Franco says tomorrow. That is (Brazil's) exchange rate policy. And what does it depend on? The president's need to have a competitive currency or maintain inflation low so that he can win a second term?"

Dornbusch said Brazil should speed currency depreciation by about five percent a year for the next five years. He said that would result in an inflation rate of about 11 percent, rather than seven percent, but it would lead to economic growth of about eight percent instead of four percent.
"Would anybody die from this? No. Could the president be re-elected? Yes.," Dornbusch said.
((--John Miller, Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511 248-5414))
